Flux Extraction

Extract and measure spectral line fluxes for a chosen target species (CO, H2, or any molecule/atom HITRAN or a custom catalog supports) from spectral data cubes. This tool analyzes emission or absorption across multiple rotational transitions of that species.

Starting Flux Extraction

Fetch from HITRAN

  1. Enter min/max wavelengths in the toolbar, then click HITRAN

  2. Choose a molecule (required)

  3. Choose isotopologue number (optional)

  4. Choose transition level (optional, different molecules have different transition levels)

  5. Refresh HITRAN cache (optional)

Seven common molecules are preloaded and ready offline, no fetch needed: H2O, CO2, CO, OH, HCN, C2H2, H2. Any other molecule is fetched live from HITRAN the first time you request it (via HAPI, version 1.3.0.0), then cached locally for next time.

52 molecules have lines in the 1–30 µm range this app targets, and support transition-level filtering (step 4 above):

CO, H2, OH, H2O, HCN, C2H2, CO2, CS, OCS, SO2, C2H6, C4H2, HC3N, CH4, NH3, CH3, H3⁺, HF, HCl, HBr, HI, N2, NO⁺, NO, ClO, O2, SO, O3, N2O, NO2, HNO3, H2CO, HOCl, H2O2, H2S, HO2, COF2, COCl2, CS2, PH3, SO3, GeH4, HCOOH, C2H4, CH3OH, CH3Cl, CH3Br, CH3CN, CH3F, CH3I, COFCl, ClNO2.

Import Lines

When HITRAN isn’t reachable, click Import Lines to load your own line list from a CSV instead. Both wavelength and species columns are required.

Once lines are loaded (either way), the spectrum shows them. Hovering over a line shows its species, wavelength, transition, and Einstein coefficients. Click Lines to open a table of every currently loaded line: detections and contaminants together, with “Detection Only”/”Contaminating Only” filters. Check/uncheck rows to change what’s plotted. Click any column header to sort by that column.

Load Contaminating Lines

Additionally (and optionally), you can mark contaminating (non-target) lines so both Flux Map and Multi-Gaussian Fit (below) can account for them instead of letting their flux distort a nearby target line’s measurement. Two ways, and they merge together:

From a CSV

  1. Click Contam. Lines and load a CSV file with unwanted lines

Both wavelength and species columns are required.

By marking one on the spectrum

  1. Click Mark Contaminant, then click the feature on the spectrum

  2. No HITRAN match is needed – it’s listed with species “N/A”

  3. The button stays toggled on so you can mark several in a row; click it again to stop

  4. To remove one, uncheck it in Lines or click its marker on the spectrum

Run Flux Map / Multi-Gaussian Fit again after loading or marking one for the fit to pick it up.

Multi-Gaussian Fit

Fit every currently-plotted line at once via curve_fit, using each line’s own instrumental width. Lines that land in the same wavelength chunk (close or blended) are fit together against one shared continuum, so they no longer double-claim overlapping flux the way independent, uninformed per-line fits would.

Each line’s starting width comes from the instrument’s own spectral resolution, but center and sigma are fitted, not fixed because each is constrained to a bounded range around that starting point (center within ±1 instrumental σ of the catalog wavelength, sigma within 0.5–2× the instrumental value), so a real line can settle slightly off its catalog center or resolve a little narrower/wider than nominal.

If you’ve loaded or marked a contaminating line (above) sharing a wavelength chunk with a requested line, it gets its own Gaussian component too, so its flux is absorbed there instead of leaking into that line’s amplitude. It’s drawn in grey on the plot and interleaved with the target lines in the results, in wavelength order. It’s never counted toward the target line total or “Total Integrated Flux”, but summed on its own as “Total Contaminant Flux” (see Reading the results below).

  1. (Optional) Fit a continuum first via Continuum Tools → Automatic Continuum → Continuum Line. If you skip this, Multi-Gaussian Fit computes one automatically the first time you click it.

  2. Click Multi-Gaussian Fit

A Gaussian curve is overlaid on the spectrum for each plotted line, and a results window opens with one block per line, an overall summary, and a separate section listing any contaminating lines that got their own component. Re-running with the same lines, contaminants, and active tab offers the cached results instead of re-fitting.

Reading the results

Each line’s block reports two groups of numbers:

  • Catalog identification — Line λ, Transition, A coeff and E_upper, copied straight from the HITRAN entry, not measured. Useful for cross-checking that the fit actually locked onto the line you think it did.

  • Fitted parameters — Center, Amplitude, Sigma, FWHM, Integrated Area and R². Center and Sigma are fitted, not fixed, but each is bounded around the catalog wavelength and the instrument’s spectral resolution respectively (see above). Units follow the same rules as the 1D page (1D Spectrum Fitting): Integrated Area is erg/s/cm² wherever the header supports the conversion.

An OVERALL summary follows every line block, e.g. from a real 56-line CO run:

OVERALL:
  Total lines fitted:    56
  Total Integrated Flux: 2.7085e-14 erg/s/cm²
  Mean R²:               0.9768
  Lines with R² >= 0.5:  56/56
  Total Contaminant Flux: 2.3774e-15 erg/s/cm²

Total Contaminant Flux only appears when a contaminating-lines catalog is loaded, and is summed separately from Total Integrated Flux (contaminants are never considered for the target total).

Contaminant lines are not grouped into a trailing section. Each one appears as its own Contam N block, interleaved with the target Line N blocks by fitted wavelength – matching where it actually sits in the spectrum, not sorted apart from the detections:

FITTED LINES (target and contaminant, by wavelength):
======================================================================
Line 1: CO
  ...
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Contam 1: H2 (not one of the 56 target lines; shown in grey on the plot)
  Center (λ):            4.410011 µm
  Amplitude:             6.3049e+03 MJy/sr
  Integrated Area:       2.9563e-16 erg/s/cm²
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Line 2: CO
  ...

Contam N numbers its own kind (1, 2, 3, …), separate from the Line N count above it – neither numbering is global across the whole listing.

How Chunking Works

Multi-Gaussian Fit does not fit each line alone. It groups nearby lines into chunks first.

A chunk is a group of lines close enough in wavelength to overlap. Lines in one chunk share one continuum. The fit solves for every line in the chunk at the same time, in one curve_fit call.

This matters because two close lines share flux where they overlap. A fit that sees only one line assigns it all of that shared flux. An independent fit of the next line then claims some of the same flux again. Together, the two fits overcount the true flux.

A joint fit avoids this. Each line in the chunk still gets its own Gaussian, but every line in the chunk fits against the same data and the same baseline at once. The fit splits overlapping flux between the lines that actually produced it, instead of double-counting it.

Lines just outside a chunk can still affect it. The fit borrows these nearby lines into the joint model too, so their tails do not leak into the chunk’s own lines. A borrowed line’s flux does not count toward the chunk it was borrowed into – it is only there to keep that chunk’s own fit honest.

The result: every plotted line, in every chunk, is fit at the same time as its neighbors. No line’s flux comes from a fit that ignored what sits next to it.

Using the API

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, fit_hitran_lines
from cube_explorer.line_catalog import load_contaminating_lines_catalog

cube = load_cube("data.fits")
contam = load_contaminating_lines_catalog("path/to/ContaminatingLines.csv")  # optional

results = fit_hitran_lines(
    wavelength=cube.wavelength,
    spectrum=cube.spectrum,
    molecule='CO',
    wavelength_min=4.40,
    wavelength_max=4.80,
    v_upper=1,              # v=1->0, same filter as the HITRAN dialog
    v_lower=0,
    header=cube.header,     # Required for the erg/s/cm2 conversion
    wave_unit=cube.wave_unit,
    contam_catalog=contam,  # omit (or None) to skip contaminant handling entirely
)

detected = [r for r in results if r['success']]
print(f"Fitted {len(detected)}/{len(results)} lines")
for r in sorted(detected, key=lambda r: r['wavelength']):
    print(f"  {r['wavelength']:.6f} um  area={r['area']:.4e} {r['area_unit']}  R2={r['r_squared']:.4f}")

Fitted 56/56 lines
  4.402940 um  area=1.7523e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9522
  4.407340 um  area=2.0514e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9760
  4.411409 um  area=3.2444e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9919
  ...
  4.773897 um  area=5.4440e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9945
  4.783681 um  area=5.0950e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9889
  4.793562 um  area=5.5141e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.9156

Run the Full-Cube Flux Map

Extract a flux map across every spatial pixel, for whichever lines are currently checked in the Lines dialog (any species – the map isn’t restricted to CO):

  1. Click on Flux Map.

  2. A popup explains that continuum subtraction runs automatically per pixel, using default parameters that work well for typical spectra. Click No to use those defaults, or Yes to open the same parameter dialog as the manual Automatic Continuum tool and set your own values instead.

  3. A preview shows the brightest pixel within your wavelength range (a sanity check before committing to a full-cube run), and exactly the checked lines that will be fit. Click YES - Extract Map to proceed.

If you’ve already run an extraction with the same wavelength range, line selection, and continuum choice, you’ll be offered the cached results instead of re-running.

Progress Monitoring

The progress dialog updates per pixel as the cube is processed.

Output Products

The Display dropdown in the results window switches between four maps, all from the same run. The flux/detection labels reflect whichever species was targeted (e.g. “CO Flux” for a CO run, “H2 Flux” for H2) – the example below used CO:

Export as FITS / Show Statistics buttons in the results window apply to whichever map is currently selected.

Inspecting Individual Pixels

With Pixel Select on (the default), clicking a pixel on any of the four maps opens that pixel’s fit:

Turn Pixel Select off to zoom/pan the map freely instead of reopening this dialog on every click.

Using the Flux API

Extract fluxes programmatically for single spectra or full data cubes, using extract_flux() and create_flux_map(), the same algorithm as the GUI’s Flux Map button.

Note

This is a different algorithm from Multi-Gaussian Fit, and the two don’t produce identical totals for the same spectrum. Both now fit lines simultaneously via the same function, so the real remaining difference isn’t the fitting method itself, it’s which lines get fit: extract_flux/create_flux_map auto-detect lines per pixel and only count one that clears a signal-to-noise threshold first (snr_threshold, default 3σ). fit_hitran_lines has no SNR gate at all: it fits whatever you selected, weak lines included. Summed over many pixels this adds up to Flux Map running systematically lower. Lowering snr_threshold would let more noise into the flux instead (a trade-off, not a fix).

Extract Flux from a Single Spectrum

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, extract_flux

cube = load_cube("data.fits")

flux_result = extract_flux(
    wavelength=cube.wavelength,
    spectrum=cube.spectrum,
    target_catalog_path="path/to/CO_catalog.ecsv",
    header=cube.header,      # Required for the erg/s/cm2 conversion
    wave_unit=cube.wave_unit,
)

print(f"Total flux: {flux_result['flux']:.4e} {flux_result['flux_unit']}")
print(f"Number of lines detected: {len(flux_result['detected_lines'])}")
print(f"Mean continuum level: {flux_result['mean_continuum']:.3f}")

Create Flux Maps

Generate flux maps for the entire data cube:

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, create_flux_map

cube = load_cube("data.fits")

# Uses HITRAN (CO by default) automatically, or pass target_catalog_path for a custom catalog
flux_map_result = create_flux_map(
    cube,
    wavelength_min=4.70, wavelength_max=4.80,
    n_jobs=4,
)

print(f"Flux map shape: {flux_map_result['flux_map'].shape}, unit: {flux_map_result['flux_unit']}")
print(f"Mean flux: {flux_map_result['flux_map'][flux_map_result['flux_map'] > 0].mean():.4e}")
print(f"Pixels with a detection: {(flux_map_result['detection_map'] > 0).sum()}")
print(f"Pixels with a contam detection: {(flux_map_result['contam_detection_map'] > 0).sum()}")
print(f"Mean contam flux: {flux_map_result['contam_flux_map'][flux_map_result['contam_flux_map'] > 0].mean():.4e}")

Continuum subtraction works the same way as extract_flux above (automatic per pixel, with the default parameters unless you pass your own via continuum_params).

Expected Catalog Format

The target catalog file should be in ECSV (Enhanced Character Separated Values) format with columns:

  • line_wave_um: Wavelength in micrometers

  • species: Molecule name (e.g., “CO”, “H2”)

  • transition: Transition description (e.g., “v=1->0, J=4->5”)

  • a: Einstein A coefficient

Columns are loaded as-is, with no validation: a file missing line_wave_um or species won’t fail at load time, only later inside the fit, as a KeyError.

Tips for Flux Extraction

  • Ensure your wavelength calibration is accurate (errors affect line identification)

  • The algorithm automatically measures line widths and integrates flux

  • For more control over individual line fits, use fit_hitran_lines() instead
